newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: Swiss insurers 1996 premiums rise five percent.
newsitem.headline: Swiss insurers 1996 premiums rise five percent.

text.p: Total premium income by private insurance companies in Switzerland rose by five percent in 1996 as life insurance business compensated for a drop in income from non-life business, its first decline since 1940, the Swiss Insurance Association (SVV) said.

The fall in non-life premiums of around one percent to 13.2 billion Swiss francs was mainly due to the deregulation of automotive liability insurance in Switzerland, but also continuing sharp competition and recession, the head of SVV's information commission Hansjoerg Frei told a news conference.
Despite the decline in direct premiums, Frei said 1996 was not regarded as a bad year by the insurance industry because there were no large-scale damage claims.
Including the financial results, which are expected to be good in 1996, Frei described 1996 as "at a minimum a satisfactory insurance year," for Switzerland's direct life and non-life business.

In the medium term, Frei said he expected annual premiums in the direct insurance business to grow by a moderate one to two percent, once the effect of the deregulation of the automotive business had eased.

The annual growth in life insurance premiums was also expected to continue around six to eight percent in the mid-term, based on continued uncertainty over social security, low interest rates and the scepticism view of Europe's monetary union, which Frei said still existed.
Total premium income in 1996 by Swiss insurers, excluding reinsurance, rose five percent to around 39.4 billion francs, according to SVV estimates.
While non-life premiums fell, life insurance premiums rose around eight percent to 26.2 billion.
Including premiums from foreign subsidiaries of Swiss insurers and reinsurance, SVV estimates a rise in total premiums by Swiss insurers of 10 percent to 109 billion francs in 1996.
While the decline in the Swiss franc against other currencies explained part of the rise, worldwide there was also a trend toward rising life insurance premiums, SVV said.

The decline in premiums from direct insurance business will have an effect on the insurance technical result and insurers will continue to reduce their costs to avoid a significant erosion of margins.
Over the next years, Frei said the insurance industry expected to reduce staffing levels by 1.0 to 1.5 percent annually, the same rate seen since 1993.
Of the total premium income for Swiss insurers of 109 billion francs, around 40 percent of income comes from non-life business, 39 percent from life business and 21 percent on reinsurance.
Geographically, 43 percent of premiums come from the European Union, 37 percent from Switzerland and 20 percent from other foreign countries.
